note: Rabban Gamliel was traveling on a ship with other Elders when he remembered he had not tithed the produce of his fields. He declared that the tenth he would later measure out was given to Yehoshua, a Levite, and that the spot where it lay was rented to him. Another tenth, the tithe for the poor, he gave to Akiva ben Yosef to acquire on behalf of the poor, again renting him the place where it lay.
why: Ulla holds that a person's field acquires property for him only when he stands next to it. Rabbi Abba objects with this incident: Yehoshua and Akiva were on the ship, far from the field, yet they acquired the tithes. Ulla dismisses the objection.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Raises this incident as an objection to Ulla.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Rabbi Abba challenges.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Travels by ship with other Elders and gives away his tithes while at sea.

people.name: Yehoshua
people.about: Yehoshua ben Hananya, a Levite, who receives the first tithe.

people.name: Akiva ben Yosef
people.about: Receives the poor man's tithe to acquire on behalf of the poor.

terms.meaning: A tenth of a farmer's produce that must be set aside. The first tithe goes to a Levite; in certain years a further tenth, the poor man's tithe, goes to the poor.

note: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for one another. One day the others asked one of them to bake, and he asked them to watch his cloak. They were careless and it was stolen. Rav Pappa held them liable to pay. The Rabbis objected, since the owner was working for them at the time, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed, until it came out that the owner had in fact been drinking beer, not baking, when the cloak was stolen. The Gemara then retells the case: it was not his turn, and he baked for them in return for their guarding his cloak.
why: The discussion has just taught that people who agree to safeguard each other's property count as paid bailees, but that a bailee is exempt when the owner is working for him. This case tests that exemption, and the retelling makes the guards paid bailees.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge who held the guards liable and was embarrassed when challenged.

people.name: The Rabbis
people.about: Challenge Rav Pappa's ruling.

terms.meaning: A rule that a person guarding another's property is exempt from paying if the owner was working for him at the time the guarding began.
Someone who looks after another's property for payment or benefit; he must pay if it is stolen or lost.

note: A man rented his donkey to another and warned him not to take the Nehar Pekod road, where there was water, but the Neresh road, where there was none. The renter took the Nehar Pekod road and the donkey died. When he came back he admitted taking that road but said there was no water there. Rava said his word should be accepted, since he could have lied and claimed he took the Neresh road. Abaye answered that this reasoning does not apply where witnesses are available. The text does not say how the case ended.
why: It comes in a run of cases about people who used or looked after someone else's property and lost it, such as a stolen cloak and a washed-away sheet. This one asks when a borrower's own account of what happened can be believed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that the renter is believed because he could have told a better lie.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Argues against Rava that the reasoning fails where witnesses can be called.

terms.meaning: A legal principle: if a person could have won with an easier false claim, his actual claim is believed, since a liar would have chosen the better story.

note: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi heard that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, owed his greatness to suffering, he said afflictions must be precious and took thirteen years of them upon himself: kidney stones and scurvy (the Gemara gives two versions of how many years of each). His stableman, said to be richer than the king of Persia, timed the feeding of the animals for when Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi went to the latrine, so their lowing would drown out his screams of pain. Even so, his cries were louder than the animals and were heard by sailors out at sea.
why: The Gemara is comparing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's suffering with Rabbi Elazar's. Right after, it says Rabbi Elazar's afflictions were greater, because they came out of love, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's came and left because of particular incidents.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; takes years of afflictions upon himself.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage whose greatness was said to come from his suffering.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: King of Persia; the stableman is said to be wealthier than he.

terms.meaning: A measure of distance, roughly a kilometer.
A disease of the gums and skin; here one of the two illnesses Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi suffered.

note: Visiting the town of the late Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked whether he had a son. He was told the son had gone astray and was hired by prostitutes. He took the young man, ordained him, and gave him to his uncle, Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya, to teach. Each day the young man said he was going home; his uncle shamed him, and he vowed to stay. Grown into a scholar, he sat in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's academy, who recognized his father's voice in his. When this son, Rabbi Yosei, died, a serpent blocked his father's burial cave. A Divine Voice said it was not because the father was greater, but because the father had endured the suffering of the cave and the son had not.
why: The Gemara is telling stories of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Elazar. A similar rescue of Rabbi Tarfon's grandson follows, and the Gemara explains why he worked so hard for wayward sons: whoever teaches Torah to another's son earns a place in the heavenly academy.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; brings the wayward son back to Torah study.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The righteous father, already dead; he had suffered in a cave.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's son, who strays and becomes a scholar.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya
people.about: Rabbi Yosei's uncle, his mother's brother, who teaches him.

terms.meaning: Given the title Rabbi; the text describes a golden cloak spread over him.
A voice from Heaven that the Sages describe announcing God's view.
Rabbi Elazar hid in a cave with his father for thirteen years to escape the Romans.

note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya sent his son to hire workers. The son hired them and promised to feed them, without saying how much. When he came back and told his father, Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya said that even a feast like King Solomon's in his time would not fulfill that promise, because the workers are descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
why: The mishna rules that workers' meals follow local custom, but an employer who promises food has added to what he owes. This incident shows how far such an open promise can reach. The Gemara then asks whether Abraham's feast really outdid Solomon's.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya
people.about: The father, who tells his son how much his promise to the workers demands.

people.name: King Solomon
people.about: Mentioned for his lavish feasts.

terms.meaning: The earliest written collection of Jewish law, which the Gemara discusses.

note: Rabba bar Rav Huna owned a forest on a riverbank, and people asked him to cut down the trees that blocked the men hauling boats along the bank. He said he would cut his trees once the owners upstream and downstream cut theirs. The Gemara asks how he could wait for others, and answers that the next forest belonged to a Persian general who would ignore a Jewish scholar, so cutting his own would achieve nothing. Rabba bar Rav Nahman sailed by, learned whose forest it was, and ordered it cut down. Rabba bar Rav Huna found it cut and cursed whoever did it: may his branches be cut down. All the years Rabba bar Rav Huna lived, Rabba bar Rav Nahman's children did not survive.
why: The Gemara has been discussing how wide a path must be cleared of trees along a river for boat haulers; Rav Natan bar Hoshaya was even beaten for demanding too much. This story shows the rule tested on a Sage's own land.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Owner of the riverside forest, who refuses to cut it alone and curses whoever does.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who orders the forest cut down; his children do not survive.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Quoted by the Gemara: improve yourself first, then others.

people.name: Parzak
people.about: A Persian general whose forest stood beside Rabba bar Rav Huna's.

terms.meaning: Men who walked along the riverbank pulling boats with ropes; trees on the bank got in their way.

note: Rav Yosef had a planter working his land who died, leaving five sons-in-law. Rav Yosef reasoned that until now he had dealt with one man, but five would rely on one another and cause him losses. He told them that if they took payment for the improvement they had made to the land and left, well and good; if not, he would remove them with no payment at all. The text does not say what they did.
why: It is one of a series of cases about planters leaving a field and whether they are paid for its improvement. Right after, Rav Yosef cites a ruling that a dead planter's heirs can be removed without that payment, and the Gemara says the law does not follow it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A landowner who wants to end his arrangement with his dead planter's heirs.

terms.meaning: A worker who plants and tends trees on another's land in return for a share, like a sharecropper.
The added value a worker's labor has given the land, which he may be owed when he leaves.

note: Runya, who planted for Ravina, caused a loss, and Ravina removed him from the field. Runya complained to Rava about what Ravina had done. Rava said Ravina had acted well. Runya protested that Ravina had not warned him first, and Rava replied that no warning was needed.
why: The Gemara has been asking whether a planter who causes a loss leaves with or without pay. The Gemara says Rava follows his own rule: teachers of children, planters, slaughterers, bloodletters and scribes count as warned in advance for any loss that cannot be undone.

people.name: Runya
people.about: Ravina's planter, removed for causing a loss.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The landowner who dismisses Runya.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules that Ravina acted rightly.

terms.meaning: A worker who plants and tends trees on another's land, like a sharecropper.
